A lovely Myst-like that checks the most important box: the puzzles are up to snuff. There's all the heavy hitters: intricate gadgets, otherworldly science, and alien pictographs. All reward thoughtful tinkering, and all are a pleasure to suss out. 

What it lacks is the world-building that the great prior art possesses. It's not that the graphics don't pop. They're as crisp as they need to be. There's just an element of surprise, visual and aural wonder, that the locations are missing. And that erodes the immersion.

The first half feels open and intertwined. Sometimes part of the challenge is simply determining which loose ends to pursue next. For this genre, that's a huge plus. But the path eventually tapers to pure linearity, one puzzle room after another, and the game suffers for it, even if those puzzles are some of the game's finest.
The story has a strong philosophical foundation, and it's written and voice-acted well, but it's told in fits and starts, and it never builds enough momentum to give weight to the moral choices in the finale.  

I hear this developer's later releases are all The Room clones. A pity, since games like this, the lonely, cerebral wandering exemplified by Myst and Riven, are far rarer birds, capable of soaring to greater heights and scratching at deeper ideas. This game doesn't nest among those peaks, but it shows the promise of developers who might one day hatch one of their own.

[b]TLDR[/b] One of the better Myst-inspired puzzle adventures, polished and more approachable, though less ambitious and lighter on narrative depth. [16/20⭐, 13h🏅(+0.5h all achievements), 3/5💡]

[b]Context[/b] Quern is a puzzle-adventure game clearly inspired by [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/macwh/recommended/63660/]the[/url] [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/macwh/recommended/63610/]Myst[/url] [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/macwh/recommended/925930/]series[/url] [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/macwh/recommended/925940/]in[/url] [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/macwh/recommended/208110/]tone[/url], aesthetics, storytelling, and structure, though its puzzle design leans much more toward escape-room logic. But among the many Myst clones (e.g., [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/macwh/recommended/493720/]Haven Moon[/url]), this is one of the most accomplished — and also one of the most approachable.

[b]Writing[/b] You control a mute protagonist who is unexpectedly transported to (the eponymous island of) Quern and stranded there against their will. Throughout the island, you follow letters and notes left by a historian studying Quern’s strange properties and using them to construct increasingly elaborate machines and portals to other worlds (which you don’t get to visit). As you progress, you also uncover fragments of the ancient civilisation that once inhabited the island.

If this sounds familiar, it’s because it very much is: Quern draws heavily from the Myst formula. Unfortunately, this is also the game’s weakest aspect in my opinion. The lore surrounding the ancient civilisation is particularly uninspired and uninteresting. The storytelling is also limited almost entirely to unidirectional notes, delivered with the same slightly pretentious tone that has become characteristic of the genre.

[b]Aesthetics[/b] The game looks good overall, with a few striking moments. However, the entire experience takes place on a single island, which makes the visual identity feel somewhat monotonous compared to the more varied worlds of its inspirations. The soundtrack is suitable, occasionally sounding almost indistinguishable from certain Myst entries. Voice acting is decent, if somewhat over-the-top — again, very much in line with the source material.

[b]Gameplay[/b] This is where Quern distinguishes itself the most from classic Myst-style games. While progression is still entirely puzzle-driven, the puzzles are generally self-contained and provide fairly clear hints, making the experience far less cryptic and frustrating than the games it imitates. There are no large-scale meta-puzzles tying the whole island together, and inventory-based interactions further reinforce the feeling of playing an escape-room game. As a result, the game flows smoothly and remains consistently approachable, even if some of the mystery and satisfaction of solving broader interconnected systems is lost in the process.

The game includes hints for inventory items (essentially indicating where they should be used), as well as a system to highlight interactable objects. Unfortunately, the latter glitched during my playthrough, occasionally highlighting incorrect locations and becoming more confusing than helpful. The game auto-saves at major progression points, but manual saves are available at any time. There are no fail states or game overs. You cannot reset or undo puzzles, though I never found this necessary.

[b]Value[/b] It took me about 13h to beat the game, and additional ~30mins to get missing achievements through save recovery (annoyingly, the game only supports 8 save slots). You can’t revisit chapters nor replay puzzles. Most achievements are tied to progression, though a few require solving puzzles correctly on the first attempt — something you are unlikely to achieve on a first playthrough, so keep strategic saves unless you want to replay portions of the game. There are multiple endings, though they depend only on last-minute choices.

Finally got around to playing this after trying out the Dimhaven demo and it's bumped Dimhaven right to the top of my most wanted list. Some sections could have been more clearly signposted, especially due to the fact that I played some sections without audio due to work meetings. However, I accept this is a personal problem and, being the first puzzle game I have played in years, could also be a skill issue...

This game has beautiful graphics, sound effects, and music, as well as an amazing storyline. One thing is for sure: this game has a lot of them.

The not recommended from me is purely based on the expectation I had for the game going into it. I was expecting a casual somewhat linear game with puzzles that would take some time and thinking, but that was not what I got. More details below.

Having said that, if you are a fan of long winded complex puzzles and exploring every nook and cranny a world has to offer, you might like this. So I'm not saying the game is bad, just not my cup of tea. I can see other people liking this more than I did.

The good:

- Graphics
- Controls
- Puzzles

The bad:

- The world
- Music
- Puzzles
- Inventory / Items
- Story


The game is somewhere between Myst, The Talos Principle and The Witness. You wake up in a world where you must... solve puzzles because a professor tells you to do so via various letter spread aound the world. That's essentially all there is to the game, solve the puzzles to get to the end.

I couldn't really think of good way to structure this review so I'll just go through the goods and bads listed above and explain why I lockered them where they are.

Lets start with the good stuff.

The game looks nice. I mean it's 10 years old by now but still looks decent. Nothing too crazy of flashy, but all the animations are solid and textures look good. I don't recall seeing anything weird during my playthrough, besides some clumsy invisible walls that limit where you can go.

Controls are solid as well. You only have a few buttons to play with anyways, but when interacting with the puzzles the game pretty much always does what you want it to do. No weird hit boxes or movements doint the opposite of what you'd want them to.

Some of the puzzles are quite nice and rewarding. You are given a variety of difficulty with these, ranging both from what logic to apply to where to even find the logic in the first place. Puzzles are listed in both good and bad for this reason.

Then the not so good

The world is just way too big with nothing in it for the most part. A lot of the game is just running from one place to another because you forgot something or have no idea where to go. I'm all for open worldish approach, but this game could have used more linearity. At times there are only very vague hints about where you need to go or where something you just solved acutally did anything. Finding those things was very frustrating to me. 90% of the world is just corridors or empty space between puzzles. After a few hours I ended up looking up a walkthrough just so I could find the puzzles instead of running around looking for them for hours.

The music is horrible. A lot of the music is just background noices that become very irritating very fast, because the tracks loop so quickly. Some areas have music but even those get annoying fast for the same reason.

Some of the puzzles in the game are so complex that there is no fun to be had with them, unless you're a hardcore puzzling fan. You might need to run from one end of the map to another to try out some of them, which again adds to the critique I had about the world earlier. Some of the puzzles are spread out so all over the place and have million moving pieces that the casual player will not have any fun with them, nor be able to solve them without a walkthrough.

I feel like missed something, but I could not tell what the items I had were. I pick something up, it goes in my inventory and I have no idea what it's even called. Some items need to be interacted with, some don't. Some need to be combined. The game does a bad job at telling you how to interact with the items if it's needed.

The story is just... something that was tossed on top of the ready game after all the puzzles were done. That's what it feels like at least. The letters you find don't really give much in terms of the story, and the only character besides you in the game that pops up just has a few minute monologue at a point in the game where the whole story is basically explained in one go. The ending is also very meh, no matter what you choose. Very unsatisfying.

So as a summary, I personally did not have fun with this game after the first hour or two. I play quite a lot of puzzle games, but this one just missed the mark for me. Too much running around, too vague hints, not enough substance as a whole. I'm sure there are people who love this type of game, but for me it just felt like an empty shell with some puzzles tossed in that had no real difficulty progression, but rather just randomly overly difficult spikes here and there, and a story that just felt like an afterthought.

I found this game waaaay late to the party, and kind of accidentally. I got recommended to wishlist their new upcoming (in 2026) game Dimhaven, because of my playtime in the DaVinci games, and was intrigued because its said "From the developers of Quern", which I had never heard of. Turn out I had, I had looked at the kickstarter a million years ago.

I grew up on games like Myst, and other similar point/click/walk puzzle games, so this was right up my alley, and I've been on a kick of these in the last few years because I could play them at my own pace.

It ultimately is a story on rails. The first half has you backtracking all over one island, building up knowledge and tools and access. The second half is in another area, but largely doesnt do a whole lot of backtracking, more linear forward momentum. It almost feels like the backhalf was written by a different team, or more rushed?  Not bad at all, but the tone shifts a lot, in playstyle and the story.

My only complaint about Quern, (of the genre too), is there is almost no-replayability because the puzzles are fixed (with the exception of 1 puzzle), so with a set of notes, or a good memory, everything after is mechanical rote. It does a good job of gating you so you cant just run to the docks and get the last page and speed run it in 30s #iykyk. 

I did a 2nd run to get some missed achievements, not stopping to smell the roses and explore every nook and cranny. first run was ~20hours, but I was exploring and taking my time. Second run just for achievement was ~3 (about what took me 12h the first time), and made it to the puzzle I missed (the one random one in the game too), which was a "do it right the first time with no mistakes" achievement (which suuucks).

tldr; If you are a fan of Myst-like games, this is worth grabbing. Make use of steam screenshots and have pen/paper near by for doodles.

If you're a fan of the Myst series, this game scratches the same itch. Puzzles are very well made and really make you think. Some of the solutions are a bit tedious and sometimes the puzzles rely on you recalling some obscure thing you saw in the past while playing. It's not immediately obvious where to look and this kinda deviates from the puzzle itself. It's not too egregious, but I did have to look up guides to get hints on some of the puzzles. 

The art style is weird in the sense that it's adequate, but the colors seem a bit washed out. Textures are repetitive and the overall world is a bit bland. The level design is top notch though, and there are still some areas that are quite awesome. This is really just nitpicking though because the game is older than the Myst and Riven remakes which are spectacular to look at.

Sound design and music are really good, but there are some areas with very loud creaking wood which can get annoying. I had to turn down ambient sound volume in those areas.

Overall, if you like puzzle games, this is a MUST play. The puzzles are incredibly well designed and complex enough to keep you thinking. The Myst inspiration is very clear and I hope the devs make more such games in the future!

What a pleasant surprise, it was really good! 

I went into it with a bit of skepticism because recently i've played Neyyah which was really horrible while promising to be a Myst like experience and people in there recommended Quern in the reviews, but Quern is on a whole different level! 

The puzzles were fun and neither too easy nor too hard, just the right amount of intriguing to be fun, while clues given to discover what to do were also well made, so discovering the whole world, area by area, hint by a hint was quite fun. 

It's also not one of the cheap games that are relying on pixelhunting and making clues easy to miss or other "puzzles by obscurity" mechanisms, and can be finished without a walkthrough reasonably without any longer blocks lasting more than a day or two of world exploration and coming back to the game until the hints click or you notice something you haven't paid attention to before. 

There were some hiccups, like the unfortunate hint for the flower recipe puzzle where you knew exactly what to do, but the presented format of the ingredients was very weird, but i'm not gonna spoil anything and the weird moments like those didn't affect the whole game experience too negatively.

The world is also pretty well made and gorgeous, and i absolutely had more "Myst-like" feeling of a good puzzle world exploration than i had with aforementioned Neyyah, despite the world being free walk real-time rendered.

If you enjoyed original Mysts you will definitely like this one!

The game is mostly solid, but there's some design decisions that got relatively close to ruining the experience for me. It's a tricky, double-edged sword to walk for puzzle games, since the solutions to the logic puzzles are honestly not super complex, having to find the correct button sequences based on info you found. The notebook mechanic is a really nice touch, it allows you to take snapshots that you can use to look up stuff without having to run all the way back, and also write your own notes and thoughts about it.

Having to hunt around for the puzzles gets a bit tedious, some solutions are REALLY far-fetched, but the one thing that truly made me deduct points for pure annoyance, was when the game asked me to memorize a sequence of FOURTEEN button inputs that had to be repeated accurately, forcing you to restart the sequence if you get one input wrong, and the sequence being random every time, Aside from a very particular niche of people, this part is actually unplayable without using tools outside of the game - I tried using the notebook for it, didn't manage to get it right.

I don't mind being stuck if I can't figure out the solution. I DO mind being stuck when I know the solution but can't overcome the challenge because my brain isn't wired for hardcore memorization. My recommendation remains positive, but this really took away from the overall experience.

TL;DR: If you love puzzle games that are challenging but not unsolvable, it's absolutely recommended.

[b]The visuals:[/b] It's really nice. With all the beautiful scenery and attention to detail, walking this world is a pleasant experience.

[b]The story:[/b] This is where the game falls a bit short. There is a decent worldbuilding and backstory that's being revealed as you play the game, but the reason you are in that world is really just an excuse plot to make you solve all those puzzles.

[b]The puzzles[/b]: Here is where the game really excels. This is the type of puzzle game where you have to think in terms of the entire game map, but without it being overwhelming. While the later part of the game is more linear and more of the classic "solve the puzzle, open the door, proceed to the next puzzle", in the larger part you explore a world that opens up as you solve the puzzles, but you shouldn't forget one area just because you already solved a puzzle there: whatever is there might become useful in a later puzzle. You have to revisit most of the areas multiple times, and you have to use many items multiple times in different contexts.

[b]The controls:[/b] I play with keyboard and mouse, and it's mostly straightforward, but I I've heard other people complaining about difficulty with the controller. There are some minor problems. Most of the interactions are just click or click and drag, which is indicated by the shape of the crosshairs, so it's usually fine. Whenever you interact with something movable, most of the times you can toggle between a few distinct positions. However, there are a few places where you have to position something in an analog way. Here, dragging makes the control go haywire and it's a nightmare to position the thing properly. The trick is to right-click, which freezes your looking direction and reveals a mouse pointer. Then, you can control these interactions fine. The problem is that while the option is always there, in most of the cases you don't have to use it.

Quern is a pleasantly surprising puzzle game. I had my misgivings at first, what with the *abysmal* performance (I should not be getting 40-60 fps at 4k with a 7900 XTX), but it turned out to be a really cozy and in depth puzzle game. I love the Myst style of being plopped on an island where you solve a bunch of puzzles in an interconnected puzzle world, and Quern executes that really well. Being able to slowly open up an island and return to places previously plodded to solve new puzzles is extremely satisfying, and gives Quern a real sense of place. The puzzles are really fun and creative, though some of them can be overly obtuse. Don't be like me, remember there is an item description button in the bottom right! Despite that I found almost every puzzle fun, except for the key mastermind puzzle. You know what you did.

The story is decent. It managed to keep me invested through the runtime of the game, providing a nice backdrop to the frozen state of the island you find yourself in. Some things are left unexplained, for example they keep talking about the "power" of Quern, but I'm not quite sure what that is minus just time not passing when in Quern. The game even has two endings!

I highly recommend this to fans of Myst-like puzzle games. It is a very solid experience, and I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it. Hurray and so on.

Okay, so it's like Myst. Except I don't get to make that comparison, really, because I don't recall exactly how Myst was; because I was a little kid when I played this game on PC and didn't understand sh*t about it; and I was a teen when I actually finished it on Nintendo DS. But the vibes are Myst...is what I'm going to assume based of screenshots of Myst. Look, if that is a useful comparison to you, cool! You like Myst? You like...Obduction? Well that's pretty much in the ballpark. Now for more details...

---

Basically Quern puts you in the shoes of an unfortunate (and unwilling, I believe, though that is unclear to me) portal traveler who finds themselves trapped on a mysterious island made of white rocks, pine trees, big white rock and pine wood houses, tons of weird mechanical devices and a load of crystals of varying colors. You quickly realize you are here to follow the guidance or a mysterious man who speaks to you from the past through letters, bringing some context to the story.

The narration is solid enough to carry you from main puzzles to main puzzle. Without saying it is the most compelling plot I ever witnessed in the genre, the voice acting is solid, and the prose is subtle enough to be both good at exposition, while remaining somewhat mysterious. And when the game does go for a big exposition dump, it ends up being used to change our perspective on the plot in a pretty drastic manner, adding some more depth to it, which is welcomed. 

Solid stuff.

That story is served by, again, very solid and competent art and level design, mixing simple and recognizable architecture, that manages to be just alien enough to be interesting to look at. The steam punk (crystal punk?) technology, with tons of unnecessary beeps and boops (I'll get to that), juxtaposed with the huge rock faces and minimalist, if not austere houses, make for an interesting place to roam around. 

And everything is tied together by a pretty chill soundtrack, composed of mostly hits, with a couple of misses here and there, in my opinion. Some themes, especially the main court one (which you will hear A LOT in the first half of the game) feel under-composed, quickly redundant and boring, while also being too short to blend in the background. Thankfully, the vast majority of the OST is very competently made, with tracks that build the mysterious atmosphere well enough. Surprisingly though, the game never really goes quiet, with each zone of the island having its own little theme, that will start whenever you move from one to the other. I feel like a little quietness here and there could have helped sometimes.

---

But what about the puzzles though? 

Well, I'm going to say I mostly had a good experience with the puzzles; which is why I recommend Quern in the first place. But I need to highlight a couple of things I really disliked, and another that I'm still debating as to how much I liked it or not:

-Out of the dozens of puzzles that composed the game, there are three that I HATED with a passion. For two of them the game expected the player to revisit puzzles they ALREADY SOLVED, to replay them with a new item; I f*cking hated that, I didn't like it, I was not a fan of it. Though it is understood, fairly early, that you will visit each place several times, puzzles should be done and discarded. I already am trying to juggle in my mind all the concurrent inventory items I have, and unresolved puzzles that might be solved by said inventory items, I cannot also be expected to keep in mind the growing list of puzzles I already solved, just for the sake of TWO OF THEM being relevant several hours later. For me, this is not clever, this is not thinking outside of the box, this is a hard "no".

As for the third puzzle, I am not even going to burry the lead, it's the Simon Says. And not only would I not be super enthusiastic about it, because at face value...it's Simon Says. But this one has the audacity to ask you to remember 14 (FOURTEEN) consecutive notes, composed of a range of five, that will be randomly composed each time you retry the puzzle. Now here is the deal: it is obviously a ridiculous task; so the only explanation possible (one that was confirmed by reading a developer talking about that puzzle in a game thread) is that you are not expected to actually play Simon Says. But you are expected to either spam the note system and then painstakingly reproduce the combination, by opening/closing the notebook 14 (FOURTEEN) times; or...to take your smartphone, the thing you are trying to forget when playing video games (I'm not particularly addicted to my smartphone, I'm just trying to be relatable here) to film your screen, and then (again) painstakingly scroll through the timeline of the video to look at each note to reproduce. This SUCKS a big dongle. Taking notes on a piece of paper is one thing. Filming my Steam Deck and then having to alternate between my phone and my Deck to enter a 14 (FOURTEEN FFS) notes combination is just silly.

To be clear, I wrote two whole paragraphs, because quite frankly, I just found it infuriating. But the reality is, it was not that much of an issue in a 14-15hrs playthrough.

-On a broader subject, I am a bit torn on the whole input system. To be clear, I played this 2016 release on Steam Deck, using both joysticks and the right trackpad like a mouse. It is very likely that keyboard and mouse make a better combo for this game. Although the game has controller support...

Basically, when it comes to the interactions with puzzles, Quern plays like a Frictional Games game: i.e you don't just push buttons, you click and drag, click and pull, click and push. The nature of the game world, the ancient and magical technology aspect of the game is remarkably extended to the machines you interact with. It is rare that Quern asks you to simply dial a code on a keyboard. You'll be pulling levers, to align arrows, making sure little LEDs are lit properly, before turning a knob somewhere else. And for the most part, that works to create tactility with the game world. Being a fan of Frictional and games like Statik on PSVR, or the Room trilogy on Android, I'm actually really happy that this is how Quern works.

The issue is just that, several puzzles became incredibly tedious to solve because of these controls.

Some of the puzzles that I ended finding tedious to solve, felt tedious because testing hypothesis took a lot of mental energy, and required a lot of button presses to get things done. Sometimes, it felt like the expected behavior for solving puzzles was to look at each part of it, then onto a piece of paper, calculating in advance your moves before testing them. I don't believe that is actually what was expected of me; but it felt like that at times. 

The worst offenders are the alignment puzzles (you move a piece another one also moves; if you move that second one, it moves a third one etc.). These are typically "fumbling" puzzles, where you fiddle around, not necessarily to stumble on the solution, but to look at the thing moving while you are doing it, so you get to a position where you see the solution a couple of moves away, and then start calculating. To be played the "fumbling" way, these require A-that you can look at it while moving pieces, and B-that you can quickly manipulate it. It's a very simple iteration on the Rubik's Cube. But with these controls, and with this admittedly lovely crystal punk aesthetic, a lot of tubes and levers, you are always in for a cumbersome interface, that sometimes is justified and enhance the puzzles, sometimes kind of ruins the solving process. 

To an extend, I recognize this is a skill issue on my part. If I was better at solving some of these puzzles, I wouldn't mind at all the fiddling. But it is what it is.

---

TL;DR
I enjoyed Quern a lot. It is well made, has three puzzles I hate and a bunch I loved solving.

Quern é um excelente jogo, praticamente a definição de um título feito para quem realmente gosta de puzzles. Sua ambientação e trilha sonora são extremamente convidativas e sustentam uma imersão constante. Como myst-like, é uma experiência que vale muito a pena.

O jogo é difícil e no geral, o puzzle design é ótimo e dá prazer de decifrar os mecanismos do jogo. Tem alguns momentos em que os desenvolvedores exageram na dificuldade e acaba ficando meio sem sentido, mas são exceções que não prejudicam a obra como um todo. As ideias são frequentemente bem criativas, e impressiona ver um projeto indie alcançar um nível de polimento tão alto.

A parte inicial chega perto de uma obra-prima em design de puzzles. Esse “primeiro ato” apresenta uma progressão quase perfeita, com puzzles difíceis na medida certa e uam boa integração com o mundo do jogo, em alguns pontos, superando o próprio Myst. Depois de algumas horas, senti que a experiência se estende além do necessário, com uma leve diluição do ritmo, mas nada que prejudique significativamente a jornada.

A narrativa facilmente é o elemento mais fraco. Não há uma história muito profunda ou surpreendente, mas ela cumpre o papel de pano de fundo funcional para a exploração e os enigmas. O desfecho também não busca um impacto extremo: é mais interpretativo, dependendo de como o jogador enxerga a responsabilidade de lidar com um poder tão grande.

Por fim, eu reforço que Quern não tenta ser outra coisa além de um jogo de enigmas, e isso é uma virtude. Quem não aprecia o gênero provavelmente vai achar lento ou muito difícil, talvez nem passando do início. Mas para quem gosta, é uma jornada excelente, com identidade clara e poucas, embora perceptíveis, imperfeições.

Quick review:
A fun puzzle game, with not a lot of hints, so you can't just breeze through it. Story rich, and leads you through the lore so you can eventually make your own decision.

What you get to play:
Quern is a puzzle game that isn't a room to room puzzle. You are brought to an island you need to "solve". These puzzles are arranged so you can unlock parts of different places. You can revisit any area (sortof) and use it (like potions or telescope) again to solve new puzzles. Very intuitive and thought through. Although the freedom is at it's highest in the first area, the lore is at it's highest in the second area.

About hints and things you can do:
Be not afraid to use the hints however. The puzzles don't always point to the next area/item. The best "first hint" is using alt to see what can be interacted with. Second, a question mark in the bottom right corner in the "items" inventory. The third, is to look around, connect logical conclusions and look for symbols. There are levers you can pull/push, pull up/push down, lights toggled on/off, ... .

For you, and 2 tips:
This game is for someone that likes puzzles, finds new logic, uses interprative meaning. It has only a few standerd "game logic" puzzles, it's more of a real world that uses magnitism, bait, weight, sequencing, music notes, "lazer" beams, ... . Be imaginative, use items where you think it might work. And don't forget 2 things. You CAN take notes with "p" and view the screenshot in your notebook and add notes. You CAN press mouse 2 to hold your screen still and move your mouse cursor like normal to solve puzzles because all of them are world interactions.

Get it:
I definitly recomend the game if you've got some puzzle sense or even mastered them. It's harder for newcommers but definitly doable. Get it on sale, around max €15.

Added notes:
It's a well thought out puzzle game, I like the lore very much, and the graphics are amazing. But it is just a one and done game. If I may compare, Outer Wilds has the same "unlock things" (knowledge) like Quern (stage progression), has the same once known/item-obtained, it's always an open world. But Quern sets it up so you can only do THAT next puzzle when you get THAT item. Sometimes you get 2, but it's mostly just a part of a key to unlock a box after some puzzles. That is how the puzzles are set up in Quern, and it's not a mistake. It just makes it seemed forced while it's just needed to be that way. Altough I'd like to play a version where the keys aren't keys, but they're.. grapling hooks. They did that right with the green crystal (you'll know later).

[h1][b]🎮 Reseña de Quern: Pensamientos Inmortales[/b][/h1]

[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
Quern: Pensamientos Inmortales es una aventura en primera persona centrada en exploración y rompecabezas, de esas que te sueltan en una isla rara, atmosférica y medio steampunk para que “descubras la verdad” mientras tu cerebro pide auxilio y tu libreta se convierte en tu mejor amiga. No es un juego de acción: es un paseo elegante entre mecanismos, puertas que no se abren porque “te falta el ítem filosófico #7”, y misterios que se te quedan pegados en la cabeza.

La primera impresión es clara: esto es para quien disfruta pensar, observar y conectar pistas. Si esperas un parque de diversiones, te equivocaste de fila. Aquí el “simulador de caminar” viene con tarea: investigar, escuchar narración, y resolver rompecabezas con lógica (y con ese toque de “sí, era obvio… después de verlo en retrospectiva”).

[h2]Lo Brillante y lo Oxidado[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
✅ Rompecabezas bien al centro de la experiencia 🧩: no están de adorno; son el juego.  
✅ Ambientación misteriosa y atmosférica 🌫️: te vende la isla y sus rarezas con ganas.  
✅ Buena narración y trama 📜: el misterio te empuja a seguir, aunque sea por puro orgullo.  
✅ Subtítulos disponibles 📝 y Steam Cloud ☁️: gracias por permitir que mi progreso no dependa de rituales.  
✅ Logros y cromos 🏆🃏: para los que necesitan validación digital por resolver una palanca.

Lo No Tan Bueno:
❌ Compatibilidad parcial con mando 🎮: perfecto si te gusta pelearte con controles “casi” cómodos.  
❌ Ritmo de “relajación” que a veces roza el letargo 💤: caminar es bonito… hasta que lo haces por quinta vez.  
❌ Si no te gustan los rompecabezas duros, esto puede sentirse como castigo académico 📚: no todos van a tener paciencia.  
❌ Comunidad activa pequeña (19 jugadores) 👥: no esperes una fiesta; esto es un club de lectura con engranes.
